hook_text: From a city you might see thirty stars. From the Karoo you can see thousands. The sky did not change. You did.
clip_script: Stand under a streetlight in town on a hazy night with a full Moon and count the stars: maybe thirty. Now drive to the Karoo on a clear winter night, no Moon, no lights for kilometres. Give your eyes twenty minutes. Thousands of stars appear, the Milky Way glows with dark lanes of dust, and the Magellanic Clouds hang like misty patches. Astronomers hunt for exactly this: darkness, dry clear air, steady air that does not make stars twinkle, and height above the haze. That is why South Africa's biggest optical telescopes moved from Cape Town, founded in 1820, to a hill near Sutherland, high, dry and dark. Radio telescopes have a different enemy: cellphone signals. So MeerKAT and the SKA sit in a protected, radio-quiet corner of the Karoo. Want to try it? Pick a new Moon night, find somewhere dark, use a red torch, and wait.
visual_style: A split whiteboard sky, left half washed out by a streetlight and full Moon with a few dots, right half packed with stars and a Milky Way band, then a map of South Africa with pins at Cape Town, Sutherland, the Karoo and Hartebeesthoek.
pacing: A striking comparison, then the reasons, then a challenge to try it.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and plan your own dark-sky night.
